extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and dramatists writing or evaluating heroic/epic plays for the stage (Restoration/early-modern style)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and staging 'heroic plays' — verse dramas modelled on epic/heroic poetry emphasizing love and valour, elevated diction, spectacular action, and occasional supernatural machinery. Covers poetic form, subject-matter, characterization, staging, and rhetorical limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of heroic verse / elevated language
rubrics_metrics.description: “Serious plays ought not to imitate conversation too nearly... If nothing were to be raised above that level, the foundation of poetry would be destroyed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serious drama should use elevated verse rather than orthodox conversational prose; this elevation permits exalted thought and imagery suitable to heroic material. Acknowledge the difficulty of writing good verse — poor verse dishonours the form — but prefer verse when possible to avoid destroying poetic dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of an heroic poem (mini-epic model)
rubrics_metrics.description: “An heroic play ought to be an imitation, in little, of an heroic poem; and, consequently, that love and valour ought to be the subject of it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the play as a condensed epic: concentrate on grand actions, noble passions, and the scope of an epic within the limits of stage structure. The laws of epic do not dispense with dramatic laws but raise them to greater heights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter: love and valour
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroic drama should chiefly treat love and valour as its principal subjects (following Ariosto: 'Le donne, i cavalier, l'arme, gli amori').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot and character motivations should centre on heroic military deeds and elevated romantic passion; these coupled elements define the heroic tone and justify ample spectacle and heightened diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fullness of plot and variety of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: A heroic play needs 'design, and variety of characters' — avoid the slender plotting and paucity of persons that hamper early attempts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a well-filled plot with multiple persons and incidents to match the grandeur expected of an epic imitation; avoid overly sparse, narrative-like works that lack dramatic variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for supernatural and magical elements
rubrics_metrics.description: “An heroic poet is not tied to a bare representation of what is true, or exceeding probable; but that he may let himself loose to visionary objects... the greatest beauties” (examples: the ghost of Polydorus, Enchanted Wood, Bower of Bliss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gods, spirits, visions, or magical machinery where they serve imaginative and thematic ends; supernatural elements are legitimate poetic devices and can enrich character and spectacle when consistent with the heroic tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of drums, trumpets and battle spectacle onstage
rubrics_metrics.description: To those who object my frequent use of drums and trumpets, and my representations of battles, I answer... these warlike instruments, and even their presentations of fighting on the stage, are no more than necessary to produce the effects of an heroic play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ martial music, staged combat, and visible military spectacle to raise the audience's imagination and convincingly persuade spectators that they witness great deeds; such devices are part of the heroic play's effect and precedent exists (e.g., Shakespeare).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevated imagination over narrow naturalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious plays should not imitate ordinary conversation too closely; poetry must be allowed to 'raise' thoughts and images above life to preserve the art's final perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept departures from strict naturalism as a necessary artistic choice for heroic drama; poetic elevation and imagined grandeur are virtues rather than defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero characterization: grandeur with amiable imperfections
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero may have 'roughness of character, impatient of injuries, and a confidence of himself, almost approaching to an arrogance' but also qualities like 'frank and noble openness... easiness to forgive... inviolable faith in his affection.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft heroes who are great and sometimes eccentric: allow faults that humanize but do not undermine their heroic stature. Flaws should be presented as part of a large, compelling character rather than mere vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive bombast and self-egotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of passages where the hero 'vaunts his own importance' and speaks with extravagant egotism that is 'hardly one of those consequences adapted to shew forth the character of a hero in theatrical representation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit passages of overblown self-praise or ranting that undermine plausibility or theatrical sympathy; passion may license elevated speech, but it should reveal character or move the plot rather than simply boast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility vs. romantic convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledges improbabilities (e.g., a single hero turning the tide of battle) but defends them as acceptable under romance conventions and historical precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the demands of plausibility with genre expectations: extraordinary feats can be allowed when the audience is habituated to chivalric/romantic conventions, but be conscious of when probability is needed for dramatic credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use supernatural apparitions to reveal character and poetic beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The ghost of Almanzor's mother is introduced to 'shew how the hero could support even an interview with an inhabitant of the other world' and to 'throw in some fine poetry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supernatural encounters should serve character exposition and poetic enrichment, not mere novelty; use them to heighten moral or emotional stakes and to insert lyric passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage pace and changes of fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: The drama's 'changes of fortune are too rapid to be either probable, or altogether pleasing, yet they arrest the attention by their splendour and importance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary incidents to keep attention, but avoid such rapid reversals that they strain plausibility or reduce emotional payoff; grand events may justify brisk changes, but pacing must preserve audience engagement and coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnificence of fable, language and action
rubrics_metrics.description: If considered as romantic poetry, 'there are few compositions... which convey a more lively and favourable display of the magnificence of fable, of language, and of action, proper to that style of composition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for rhetorical splendour, rich imagery, and elevated acts that together produce an impression of magnificence; ornamentation and high diction are features to be cultivated in heroic plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide contextual/local anchors when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique that though characters are called Moors, 'there is scarce any expression, or allusion, which can fix the reader's attention upon their locality' — a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include occasional local expressions, cultural references, or patriotic sentiment to ground setting and stakes when the historical or national context is relevant to the drama's conflict; avoid generic or placeless presentation where setting matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhyme and form: accept the difficulty but favour rhyme
rubrics_metrics.description: Defense of rhyme: 'It is indeed so difficult to write verse... Yet, even they who have written worst in it, would have written worse without it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhyme (where appropriate for heroic verse) despite its difficulty because it can elevate and refine expression; be mindful that poor rhyme can mislead listeners by sound alone, so strive for both technical skill and truthful sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate musical/recitative elements where they enhance heroic presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: D'Avenant introduced recitative music and scenes from Italian opera as adornments; such devices came from opera and heightened examples of moral virtue in verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where suitable, deploy musical or operatic techniques (recitative, scenic music) to amplify heroic tone and to assist presentation of exalted material; adapt operatic devices to dramatic needs rather than mimicry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic persuasive purpose: command the audience's imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet is to 'endeavour an absolute dominion over the minds of the spectators; for, though our fancy will concur...' and must 'persuade them, for the time, that what they behold on the theatre is really performed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design all elements (language, spectacle, music, pacing) to secure suspension of disbelief and to persuade the audience to accept the play's heightened reality for its duration; theatrical art aims to dominate the spectators' fancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Didactic aim: heroic poetry should inspire virtue in the great
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Heroic poesy has always been sacred to princes, and to heroes... that kind of poesy, which excites to virtue the greatest men, is of the greatest use to human kind.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider a moral or exemplary function: present heroes in a way that serves as imitation and instruction for noble persons, addressing princes and leaders as patrons and exemplars.
